lesson.title: Structure: arcs and turning scenes

lead.text: Go back to the film and its marks out of ten. Write the marks in a row and draw a line through them, and the line behaves like a walk across hilly ground. It starts low and climbs for most of the way. Then it reaches a summit and comes down on the other side. The sketch below does this for two stories you may know, with one bar for each scene.

afterFigure.text: The summit is the climax, the point where a story reaches its greatest height. Before it, the fortunes of the main character, who is called the protagonist, are mostly climbing. After it they fall. Finding the climax is the first skill in this lesson, and it needs only two moves. Read the height of each scene, then pick the highest.
In everyday speech a climax can mean any exciting moment. Here the word has a narrower sense. It means the top of the hill, and a story has only one.

model.title: Little Red Riding Hood in six scenes

lead.text: Here is a film scored the way the opener described, with one mark out of ten for each of five scenes. Use the summit test from the last screen.

reveal.text: Scene 4 scores 9, the highest mark. After it the tension eases to 5, so the film reaches its peak in the fourth scene and falls away.

lead.text: In 1863 the German writer Gustav Freytag studied how the plays of ancient Greece and of Shakespeare were put together, and described the pattern he found in a five-act play. He drew it as a pyramid, which is the hill from the last screen with straight sides. The pyramid has five parts, and each has a name.

The first part sets out the world before anything happens, with its place, its time and its people. Freytag called it the introduction, and English critics usually call it the exposition. Next comes the rising action, a run of events in which the protagonist’s fortunes climb and the trouble tightens. At the top sits the climax. After the climax, the falling action carries events downhill until the play ends in the catastrophe, the final stroke that settles the protagonist’s fate.

afterFigure.text: “Catastrophe” sounds like a disaster, and in a tragedy it is, because the hero falls. In other kinds of story the same place in the pyramid is called the resolution or the denouement, and it may be a happy one. A comedy, for example, rises again at its end towards a wedding or a reunion. The five names hold for every plot, and they let you say where in a story any event belongs.

scenes.label: Rising: the wolf in the wood

lead.text: One part of the pyramid comes before any conflict starts. In Romeo and Juliet it would hold an Italian city where swords are worn and quarrels flare, ruled by a prince who keeps the peace with difficulty.

reveal.text: The exposition, which Freytag called the introduction. It sets out the world before the action starts and ends when something disturbs it, such as Romeo and his friends deciding to go to the Capulet feast.

steps.headline: Romeo and Juliet in five acts

lead.text: Freytag applied his pyramid to Shakespeare, so Romeo and Juliet makes a good test. In Act 1 two families, the Montagues and the Capulets, are at feud. Romeo, a Montague, goes uninvited to a Capulet feast and falls in love with Juliet. In Act 2 they meet again in a garden at night and are secretly married the next day.

Act 3 begins with a street fight in which Tybalt, Juliet’s cousin, kills Romeo’s friend Mercutio. Romeo kills Tybalt in revenge, and the prince banishes him from the city. The newly married lovers have one night together before he must leave. Their luck has been climbing since the feast.

In Act 4 Juliet is told to marry another man, and she takes a drink from Friar Laurence that will make her seem dead for more than a day. In Act 5 a message to Romeo goes astray. He hears that she is dead and dies beside her in the tomb, and Juliet wakes to find him gone and takes her own life. Read the story with the pyramid in mind. Everything before the climax climbs, and everything after it falls.
Freytag counted the play’s five acts and put one of them at the top of his pyramid. Use the story you have just read to say which.

reveal.text: Act 3. Freytag traces the rise through the masked ball, the garden, the wedding and Tybalt’s death. He sets the climax in Act 3, from Juliet’s “Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds” to Romeo’s farewell. Everything after it descends towards the tomb.

model.title: Romeo and Juliet by act, after Freytag

scenes.label: Act 3: Tybalt dies; the wedding night

lead.text: The pyramid works act by act. A closer look goes scene by scene and asks something different: has this scene changed anything for the protagonist? To answer, give each scene a value, either hope (+) or loss (−), at its start and again at its end. A scene might begin with the lovers hopeful and end with one of them banished.

When a scene ends on a different value from the one it began with, it is a turning scene: it has turned the story from hope to loss or from loss to hope. Where the two values match, the scene builds or confirms what was already so. A balcony meeting that begins in hope and ends in more hope has turned nothing, even if it moves us.

afterFigure.text: In the sketch above, Cinderella has three turning scenes. The fairy godmother turns loss into hope. Midnight turns it back, and the slipper hunt reverses it again. Red Riding Hood has two. Counting turning scenes shows where a story is busiest. A play in which every scene turned would be exhausting, and one in which none did would stand still.

model.title: Little Red Riding Hood in six scenes

lead.text: Here is the same test on bare signs. Each scene is written as its opening value, then its closing value.

reveal.text: Two. The first scene turns hope into loss and the second turns loss into hope. The third opens and closes at +, so it holds.

lead.text: The figure gives eight scenes of Romeo and Juliet, with the lovers’ value at the start and end of each. Apply the same test to every scene.

reveal.text: Five of the eight turn. The tomb opens in loss and stays there, and the balcony and the wedding hold their hope.

lead.text: Look again at the eight scenes you just checked. The five that turn are not spread evenly. The feast turns loss into hope, and then the lovers hold their hope through the balcony and the wedding. After the wedding the turns come thick and fast, four in the second half of the play.

Put this beside the pyramid and the two views agree. The climax in Act 3 sits where those turns begin, and the falling action is the stretch in which they keep coming. The pyramid names the parts of the shape, and the turning scenes show what the shape is made of: one change after another in the protagonists’ fortunes.

Both tests work on a story you have never read. Score the scenes and find the highest, then read the signs to see where the story changes. The last question asks for the first of these on a heist film.
Here is a story you have not met, a heist film in six scenes. The bars show how far the action has climbed in each one. Apply the first test, and give the scene’s number counting from the left.

reveal.text: Scene 4, the alarm. The chase and the split are falling action, and the last scene works as the catastrophe or resolution. Comedies use the same shape with the ending reversed, rising again to a marriage or a reunion.

lesson.orientation: Map a play onto Freytag's pyramid, find its climax, and count the scenes that turn a value from hope to loss or back.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: Think of a film you know well and lay its scenes out in order, the way chapters sit on a shelf. Now give each scene a mark out of ten for how tense it is. The marks will not be random. The opening scenes usually score low and the middle ones climb, and somewhere near the end there is a scene that scores higher than all the rest.

Not every story builds in the same way, yet nearly all of them have a shape that can be drawn. A plot rises, reaches a high point and falls away. The shape tells you which scene matters most and how long the story takes to wind down after it.

This lesson draws that shape for a play. It starts with a simple way to score a story and goes on to the names a nineteenth-century German critic gave to its parts. It ends by checking which scenes of Romeo and Juliet change the lovers’ luck.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll find the high point of a plot, name its parts and count the scenes that change a story’s course.

recap.keyIdea: A plot climbs to a highest point and falls away. Freytag’s pyramid names the parts, and the scenes whose value changes show where the story moves.

blocks.text: You found the tensest of five film scenes and placed the climax of Romeo and Juliet in Act 3. You counted five turning scenes among its eight and found the alarm as the climax of a heist in six scenes. The film you scored at the start turned out to have the same hill-shaped outline as the plays.

recap.nextHook: You now have the tools to read a sentence, an argument, a poem and a story. Pick a text of your own and try them on it.

questions.prompt: Romeo and Juliet has five acts. In which act does Freytag place its climax, the high point after which the action turns against the lovers?
hints: Think back to the point where the lovers’ luck stops climbing.
Which act holds Tybalt’s death and Romeo’s banishment?
Count the acts up to that one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Act 3. Freytag treats Tybalt's death as the end of the rise and the scene group from 'Gallop apace' to Romeo's farewell as the climax.

questions.onCorrect: Act 3. Freytag ends the rise with Tybalt's death and places the climax from “Gallop apace” to Romeo's farewell.

misconceptions.feedback: Act 1 is the introduction. The climax comes where the rise ends and the fall begins.
Act 5 is the tomb, where the play ends. The climax comes earlier.
Act 2 is still rising. Find the act where Romeo kills Tybalt and the lovers part.
Act 4 already falls. The climax comes just before it.

questions.prompt: Name the part of Freytag's pyramid that introduces the place, the time and the people before the conflict begins.
hints: It comes first and explains the situation.
questions.onCorrect: The exposition, Freytag's “Einleitung” or introduction, sets out the world before the action starts.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a later part. The part asked for comes first, before the conflict begins.

questions.prompt: The diagram gives eight scenes of Romeo and Juliet, each opening and closing with a value for the lovers, + or −. A scene turns when its closing value differs from its opening value. How many of the eight scenes turn?
hints: Read each scene's opening and closing sign.
A scene that opens + and closes + does not turn.
Count the scenes whose two signs differ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five: 1.5, 3.1, 3.5, 4.1 and 5.1. The balcony, the wedding and the tomb hold their value.

questions.onCorrect: Five: scenes 1.5, 3.1, 3.5, 4.1 and 5.1 change value. The balcony, the wedding and the tomb hold theirs.

misconceptions.feedback: Check scene 4.1 again: it opens at − and closes at +.
More scenes than that change value. Compare each scene's two signs.
That counts every scene. Count only those whose signs differ.
One of the scenes you counted holds its value. Compare the signs again.

questions.prompt: The diagram plots how high the action has climbed in each of six numbered scenes of a heist story. Which scene is the climax?
hints: Freytag's climax is the highest point of the pyramid.
Compare the heights of the scene markers.
Give the scene's number, counting from the left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Scene 4, the alarm: the action peaks there and every later scene descends.

questions.onCorrect: Scene 4, the alarm: the action peaks there and every later scene descends.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the height, not the scene's number. Give the scene.
Scene 6 is the last scene. The climax is the highest point.
Scene 3 is high, but a later scene is higher.

questions.prompt: In Freytag's scheme, what is the final part of a tragedy, in which the hero falls, called?
hints: The Greek word means an overturning.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The catastrophe, Freytag's 'Katastrophe'; in other plots the same position is called the denouement or resolution.

questions.onCorrect: The catastrophe, Freytag's “Katastrophe”. In other plots the same position is called the denouement or resolution.

misconceptions.feedback: The climax comes earlier, when fortunes turn. The final part comes after it.
The fall comes before the final part. Name the part that closes the play.

questions.prompt: Romeo is banished at the end of 3.1, and Juliet takes the Friar's potion in Act 4. Where do these events sit on Freytag's pyramid?
hints: Do they come before or after the climax?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Falling action: after the climax, events carry the lovers down towards the catastrophe.

questions.onCorrect: Falling action: after the climax, events carry the lovers down towards the catastrophe.

misconceptions.feedback: Rising action comes before the climax. These events come after it.
Exposition opens the play. These events come late in it.

questions.prompt: A film's tension in five scenes runs 1, 3, 6, 9, 5. Which scene is the tensest?
hints: Read the five numbers in order.
Which number is the largest?
Give that number's place in the list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Scene 4: its tension of 9 is the highest.

questions.onCorrect: Scene 4. The peak is the point where the story stops building and starts to ease.

misconceptions.feedback: Scene 5 comes after the peak. Find the scene with the highest number.
That is the tension, not the scene number. Give the scene.
Scene 3 is high, but another scene is higher.

questions.prompt: At which part of Freytag's pyramid do the protagonist's fortunes stop rising and start to fall?
hints: Think of the peak of the pyramid.
questions.onCorrect: The climax is the highest point of the pyramid. Before it fortunes rise, and after it they fall.

misconceptions.feedback: The rise leads up to that point. Name the point itself.
Those come after the high point. Name the point where the turn happens.

questions.prompt: A story's three scenes run: + to −, − to +, + to +. How many of them turn?
hints: Write each scene's opening sign and closing sign.
A scene turns when the two signs differ.
Count the scenes whose signs differ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the first and the second change value. The third opens and closes at +.

questions.onCorrect: Two. A scene turns only when its closing value differs from its opening value.

misconceptions.feedback: The third scene opens and closes at the same value, so it holds.
Check each scene's two signs: more than one differs.
Compare each scene's opening and closing signs.

questions.prompt: Another story's four scenes run: − to +, + to +, + to −, − to −. How many of them turn?
hints: Write each scene's opening sign and closing sign.
A scene turns when the two signs differ.
Count the scenes whose signs differ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the first and third change value.

questions.onCorrect: Two: the first and third change value, while the second and fourth hold theirs.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare each scene's two signs. Some are the same at both ends.
The last scene opens and closes at the same value, so it does not turn.
More than one scene changes value. Compare each scene's signs.

questions.prompt: Why is scene 3 the climax rather than scene 6?

acceptedIdeas: Fortunes rise until scene 3 and fall after it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fortunes rise until scene 3 and fall afterwards.

choices.label: Fortunes rise until scene 3 and fall after it.

questions.onCorrect: The climax is the highest point: the story builds up to it and falls away afterwards.

misconceptions.feedback: Position is not the test. Ask where the heights stop rising.
Nothing here measures how long a scene lasts. Look at the heights.
